lesson.menu_title: Small Talk -- What’s Safe to Ask Where
lesson.menu_desc: A Dutchman who answers how are you honestly, an Indian auntie who asks about your salary and an American at a cooking class in Lisbon. Tonight, the little words that keep small talk going -- and the questions that are safe in each culture
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 19 -- Small Talk -- What’s Safe to Ask Where
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Claudia Veraldi | Lesson 19 -- Small Talk -- What’s Safe to Ask Where

listenings.text: Hi, I'm Pieter, and I live in Utrecht, in the Netherlands. People say the Dutch are very direct, and well, it's true. We are not great at small talk. At a party, I might ask you how much you paid for your house, or why you don't have children. For us, these questions are harmless. I mean, we are just curious. The first time I visited a friend in Texas, a woman at the supermarket asked me, how are you doing? So I told her. My back hurt, my flight was late, and I missed my wife. She just smiled and walked away. Actually, she did not want an answer at all. It was just hello. By the way, the weather is the one topic that is safe everywhere, even in Holland, because it is always bad. Anyway, now when an American asks me how I am, I say, good, thanks, and you? Ten seconds. Done.

Hello, I'm Priya. I grew up in Chennai, in the south of India, and now I live in London. In India, small talk is very personal. An auntie you meet at a wedding will ask, are you married? Why not? How much does your husband earn? It is not rude. It is a way of saying, I care about you. In London, I learned that those questions are off-limits. You do not ask about money, age or religion. So what do the British talk about? Well, the weather, the trains, and the weather again. At first, I thought it was boring. I mean, who cares if it is raining? But then I understood. The weather is common ground. Everybody has an opinion, and nobody gets hurt. Actually, now I am the one who starts. When there is a lull in the conversation, I say, lovely day, isn't it? Even when it isn't.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: To try to find out about somebody's private life
Not able to hurt or offend anybody
Light, friendly conversation about easy topics
A friendly feeling of understanding between two people
Asking about things that are too private
A short, quiet moment when nobody is talking
Interests or experiences that two people share
Not allowed; a topic you should not talk about

vocab.text: Three of tonight’s words are whole expressions: to break the ice, to keep the ball rolling and to touch a nerve. Notice the pair harmless and intrusive: every small-talk question sits somewhere between them — and the line moves from country to country.

items.situation: You meet someone at a party and there is a lull. Say something to keep the ball rolling.
tips: So, how do you know the host? / Have you tried the food? It’s great.
An open, harmless question is the safest way back in.

items.situation: Someone asks how old your house is. You are not sure. Buy some time and answer.
tips: Well, let me see... about eighty years, I think.
Well and let me see give you a second to think.

items.situation: You are talking about coffee. Move to a new topic that is connected to coffee.
tips: Speaking of coffee, have you ever been to Brazil?
Speaking of + the last topic = a smooth bridge.

items.situation: A Dutch friend asks how much you paid for your car. Answer politely without giving the number.
tips: Well, more than I wanted to! Actually, that’s a long story.
Humor + a soft change of topic. No need to be offended.

items.situation: You have to leave the conversation. Close it politely.
tips: Anyway, I should get going. It was really nice talking to you.
Anyway is the classic signal that the chat is ending.

items.situation: Tell me one question that is harmless in Brazil but intrusive somewhere else.
tips: In Brazil we ask, are you married? In England, that can feel intrusive.
This one has no grammar target. Say the true thing.

answerkey.title: Reveal the answer key
key: well / let me see = I need a second to think: Well, let me see... about ten years.
I mean = let me explain or correct: It’s small. I mean, it’s not tiny.
actually = a surprise, or a polite “no”: Actually, I’m from the interior.
by the way = a new topic, no link: By the way, where are you from?
speaking of + noun = a new topic, linked to the last one: Speaking of food...
anyway = back to the main topic, or the signal that you are leaving.
One or two of these per sentence is natural. Five in a row sounds nervous.
And the one that is not grammar: weather, food and travel are safe almost everywhere; money, age, religion and family depend on WHERE you are. When in doubt, ask about the weather.

lesson.grammar_point: connectors and fluency fillers for small talk: well, I mean, actually, by the way, speaking of and anyway
